course_title: Cisco Certified Internetwork Expert (CCIE) Enterprise Infrastructure
chapter_title: First Hop Redundancy Protocols (FHRP): HSRP, VRRP, GLBP
chapter_summary:
In any robust enterprise network, the default gateway is a critical point of failure. If the router providing the default gateway for a subnet goes down, all hosts on that subnet lose connectivity to other networks, including the internet. First Hop Redundancy Protocols (FHRPs) are designed to eliminate this single point of failure by providing an always-available default gateway, even if the primary physical router fails. They achieve this by presenting a "virtual" router to the end hosts, which is backed by two or more physical routers. If the active physical router fails, another standby router seamlessly takes over the virtual router's identity, ensuring uninterrupted connectivity for the end devices. This transparency to the end hosts is key: they continue to use the same virtual IP and MAC address, unaware of the underlying physical router switchover.

**Hot Standby Router Protocol (HSRP)** is a Cisco proprietary FHRP that provides default gateway redundancy. It works by designating one router as the "active" router and another as the "standby" router for a given HSRP group. The active router forwards traffic for the virtual IP address, while the standby router monitors the active router and takes over if it fails. End hosts are configured with the virtual IP address as their default gateway. HSRP uses a virtual MAC address (0000.0C07.ACxx, where xx is the HSRP group number) to facilitate the seamless failover. Routers communicate using HSRP hellos (UDP 1985) to monitor each other's status. Preemption is a crucial HSRP feature, allowing a higher-priority router to take over as active once it recovers from a failure. Interface tracking can also be configured to decrement a router's HSRP priority if a critical interface (e.g., the WAN link) goes down, forcing a failover even if the router itself is still operational.
Configuration example:
```cisco
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip address 192.168.1.10 255.255.255.0
 standby 1 ip 192.168.1.1
 standby 1 priority 120
 standby 1 preempt
 standby 1 track GigabitEthernet0/0 20 # Decrement priority by 20 if G0/0 fails
```
Here, `standby 1` refers to HSRP group 1. `192.168.1.1` is the virtual IP. Priority determines which router becomes active (higher is better). `preempt` allows a higher-priority router to take over.

**Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol (VRRP)** is an open-standard alternative to HSRP, defined in RFC 3768. Its operation is very similar to HSRP, using a "master" router to forward traffic and "backup" routers to take over in case of failure. VRRP also uses a virtual IP address and a virtual MAC address (0000.5E00.01xx, where xx is the VRRP group ID). The key difference from HSRP is that the master router can also use its physical IP address, unlike HSRP where the active router only uses the virtual IP. This allows the master to act as the default gateway for its own traffic, which can simplify some routing designs. VRRP also uses priorities to elect the master, and preemption is configurable.
Configuration example:
```cisco
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip address 192.168.1.10 255.255.255.0
 vrrp 1 ip 192.168.1.1
 vrrp 1 priority 120
 vrrp 1 preempt
```
VRRP is often preferred in multi-vendor environments due to its open-standard nature.

**Gateway Load Balancing Protocol (GLBP)** is another Cisco proprietary FHRP that goes beyond simple redundancy by providing true load balancing. Unlike HSRP and VRRP, which have a single active router for a virtual IP, GLBP allows multiple routers to be active simultaneously for the *same* virtual IP address. It achieves this by assigning a single virtual IP address but multiple virtual MAC addresses to the GLBP group. One router is elected as the Active Virtual Gateway (AVG), which answers ARP requests for the virtual IP. The AVG then assigns a different virtual MAC address to each of the other routers in the group, which become Active Virtual Forwarders (AVFs). When hosts send ARP requests for the default gateway (the virtual IP), the AVG responds with one of the virtual MAC addresses in a round-robin fashion (or weighted, or host-dependent), effectively distributing traffic across multiple physical routers. This provides both redundancy and efficient utilization of all available gateway resources.
Configuration example:
```cisco
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip address 192.168.1.10 255.255.255.0
 glbp 1 ip 192.168.1.1
 glbp 1 priority 120
 glbp 1 preempt
 glbp 1 load-balancing round-robin
```
GLBP is ideal for scenarios where you want to maximize bandwidth utilization and avoid having idle standby routers.

Troubleshooting FHRPs involves checking the state of the virtual router, verifying priorities and preemption settings, and ensuring communication between FHRP group members. Commands like `show standby brief`, `show vrrp brief`, and `show glbp brief` provide quick overviews of the group status, active/standby roles, and virtual IPs/MACs. If a router isn't becoming active as expected, check its priority and preemption settings. Ensure that HSRP/VRRP/GLBP hellos are not blocked by ACLs or firewalls. Authentication can also be configured (e.g., `standby 1 authentication md5 key-string cohortia`) to secure FHRP messages, and mismatches will prevent proper operation. A common mistake is forgetting to enable preemption, which means a higher-priority router won't automatically take over after recovering, leaving a lower-priority router as active. Another is misconfiguring interface tracking, causing unintended failovers or preventing necessary ones. Always verify connectivity from end hosts after making FHRP changes.

screens.title: First Hop Redundancy Protocols
screens.subtitle: HSRP, VRRP, GLBP — keeping the default gateway available and efficient

narration.text: Networks depend on the default gateway. When that single router fails, hosts lose connectivity to other subnets and the internet. First Hop Redundancy Protocols remove that single point of failure by presenting a virtual router across multiple physical devices. In practice, FHRP gives hosts a stable virtual IP and virtual MAC, while physical routers coordinate to forward traffic and take over if the primary fails. In this lesson you will learn how HSRP provides active‑standby redundancy, how VRRP offers an open standard alternative with similar behavior, and how GLBP enables active‑active load balancing by assigning multiple virtual MACs. We'll also walk through configuration examples for each protocol, show verification commands you can use, and highlight common operational pitfalls like preemption omissions and interface‑tracking surprises. By the end you'll understand not just commands but the why — when to choose HSRP, VRRP, or GLBP and how to verify resilient behavior in the lab or production.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: FHRPs create a virtual gateway so hosts never need to change their default gateway when a physical router fails; choose HSRP, VRRP, or GLBP based on vendor, feature needs, and whether you want load balancing.

First Hop Redundancy Protocols

Learn how virtual routers prevent gateway downtime, the differences between HSRP, VRRP and GLBP, and how to configure and verify each protocol so client traffic keeps flowing during failures.

In this lesson
Why gateways fail and how FHRPs keep them available
HSRP
Cisco active/standby gateway redundancy with virtual MACs and preemption.

Active‑active load balancing using multiple virtual MACs answered by the AVG.

Second, you will be able to distinguish HSRP, VRRP and GLBP in operation and when to use each, focusing on vendor scope, active‑standby versus active‑active behavior, and virtual MAC mechanics. Third, you will configure HSRP on a router to create an active and standby gateway, including priorities, preemption, and interface tracking so failover follows link health as well as device state. Fourth, you will implement VRRP as the open standard alternative and explain the key operational difference that lets the master use its own physical IP address. Each objective includes a small verification milestone so you can confirm competency in a lab. These skills let you choose, deploy and validate the right FHRP for an enterprise subnet.

screens.title: Why a virtual gateway matters
screens.subtitle: Eliminating the single point of failure at the default gateway

narration.text: A default gateway is the path a host uses to reach other networks. If that single physical router fails, every host on the subnet loses external connectivity. First Hop Redundancy Protocols solve this by presenting a virtual router — a virtual IP address and a virtual MAC — to hosts. The virtual router is a shared identity that two or more physical routers back. One router forwards traffic for the virtual address while others stand ready to take over. This makes failover transparent to end devices; they keep the same gateway address and need no reconfiguration. A common misconception is that FHRP moves a host's IP to another box. It doesn't. Hosts keep the same gateway IP; the routers share that address and coordinate. Another useful point is that virtual MAC addresses let switches keep correct L2 forwarding without host ARP changes when failover occurs. Example: if Router A fails, Router B assumes the virtual MAC and continues forwarding. Your key verification steps are simple: ping a remote host through the gateway, simulate a router failure, and confirm connectivity persists. Why does this matter? Because high availability at the gateway prevents large-scale outages and supports resilient enterprise designs.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A virtual gateway is a shared IP and MAC presented by FHRP so hosts experience continuous default routing despite physical router failures.

content.html:
Core Concept

Why a virtual gateway matters

A virtual router reduces outage risk by keeping a stable gateway identity that can be assumed by another router without host changes.

  • Transparent failover: hosts keep the same gateway IP and MAC.
  • Switches continue L2 forwarding using the virtual MAC, avoiding re-ARP storms.
  • Misconception: FHRP does not move host IPs; it moves gateway ownership between routers.
Example
Router A fails; Router B takes the virtual MAC and virtual IP. Clients continue without change.
Key Takeaway
Virtual gateways preserve connectivity and simplify host configuration during outages.
Diagram
Virtual Identity
A virtual IP and virtual MAC represent the gateway to hosts. Multiple routers advertise and back this identity.
State Coordination
Routers exchange hello messages to report electable roles and health; these determine who forwards traffic.
Operational Tip
Always verify forwarding and the virtual MAC on the switch MAC table after configuration to confirm transparent failover.

screens.title: HSRP fundamentals
screens.subtitle: Active/standby gateway redundancy, priorities, preemption, and tracking

narration.text: HSRP is a Cisco‑proprietary First Hop Redundancy Protocol that creates an active router and one or more standby routers to protect the default gateway. It presents a virtual IP and a Cisco virtual MAC that contains the HSRP group number. The active router handles forwarding for the virtual IP while standbys monitor that active using periodic hello messages. Priority values determine role election; the router with the highest priority becomes active. Preemption is a feature you must explicitly enable when you want a higher‑priority router to take back the active role after it recovers. Interface tracking lets you decrement HSRP priority when a monitored interface fails — for example, lowering priority if the WAN link goes down so a healthier router becomes active. A concrete configuration example uses the standby commands on an interface to set virtual IP, priority, preempt, and tracking. Common misconfigurations include forgetting preempt, which prevents the intended primary from regaining active status, and mismatched group numbers or authentication, which stops HSRP hellos. Confirm HSRP behavior with show standby brief to view group, role, and virtual IP information. How will you verify your HSRP design in the lab? Simulate link failures and observe role changes and the switch MAC table.

keyIdea.title: HSRP core
keyIdea.text: HSRP provides active/standby redundancy with virtual IP/MAC, uses priority and preemption for election, and supports interface tracking to make failover link-aware.

content.html:
Definition

HSRP fundamentals

HSRP designates an active router to forward for a virtual IP while standby routers take over if that active fails.

Priority: Higher priority wins the active role; default tie-breaker is IP address.
Preempt: When enabled, a higher priority router will take back active role after recovery.
Interface tracking: Decrements priority based on interface status so failover follows link health.
Example
HSRP uses a virtual MAC like 0000.0C07.ACxx where xx is the group number.
Common mistake
Not enabling preempt leaves a recovered higher‑priority router passive until manual intervention.
Verification
Show command
Use show standby brief to view HSRP groups, active/standby roles and virtual IPs.
Quick checklist
  • Confirm matching HSRP group numbers and virtual IP on both routers.
  • Verify priorities and that preempt is configured where expected.
  • Check interface tracking entries to ensure they decrement priority appropriately.

screens.title: HSRP configuration example
screens.subtitle: Configure virtual IP, priority, preempt, and tracking

narration.text: Let's walk through a standard HSRP configuration example so you can see each command's purpose. You configure the client‑facing interface with its physical address, then add standby commands to create HSRP group membership, set the virtual IP, and control election behavior. The standby ip command assigns the virtual IP that clients use as their gateway. The standby priority command raises or lowers a router's chance to become active. The standby preempt command permits a router with higher priority to recover into the active role after a failure. Interface tracking attaches a monitored interface to HSRP behavior by decrementing the priority when that interface fails, forcing a failover if necessary. A practical check after entering these commands is to run show standby brief to confirm that the intended router is active and that the virtual IP and virtual MAC match expectations. Common troubleshooting steps include verifying interface IP addresses, ensuring group numbers match, confirming that ACLs or firewalls do not block HSRP hellos, and validating tracking configuration. This example demonstrates the core operational controls you will use daily in the field.

keyIdea.title: HSRP config
keyIdea.text: Configure interface IP, standby virtual IP, priority and preempt, plus interface tracking to make router election reflect link health.

content.html:
Process Flow

HSRP configuration example

This code block shows the exact commands used on an interface to enable HSRP group 1 with tracking and preemption.

interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip address 192.168.1.10 255.255.255.0
 standby 1 ip 192.168.1.1
 standby 1 priority 120
 standby 1 preempt
 standby 1 track GigabitEthernet0/0 20
Explanation: The physical IP is assigned first, then the virtual IP with group 1. Priority and preempt control election behavior; tracking decrements priority by 20 if the specified interface fails.
Verify: Run show standby brief to confirm active/standby roles and the virtual MAC format 0000.0C07.ACxx.
Notes & Tips
Preempt: Enable where you want the intended primary to become active automatically after recovery.
Tracking: Use to avoid having a router act as gateway when its path to upstream is down.
Hell o messages: HSRP uses UDP 1985; ensure network devices do not block these messages.
Key Takeaway

Use priority, preempt and interface tracking together to achieve predictable, link-aware failover for HSRP.

screens.title: VRRP vs HSRP — practical differences
screens.subtitle: Open standard VRRP compared to Cisco HSRP behavior and use cases

narration.text: VRRP is an open‑standard alternative to HSRP. Operationally both present a virtual IP and elect a forwarding router, but there are practical differences you must understand when designing multi‑vendor networks. One key difference is that a VRRP master router can still use its own physical IP address for local traffic, whereas in HSRP the active router primarily forwards for the virtual IP. VRRP's virtual MAC format differs from HSRP's; VRRP uses a format beginning with 0000.5E00.01 and appends the group ID. VRRP also uses priorities and supports configurable preemption, so you can control which router becomes master. Use VRRP in environments with routers from different vendors because it is standardized. A common misconception is that VRRP and HSRP are interchangeable without design changes — they are similar but details like MAC format, default timers, and integration with vendor features can affect behavior. Test failover and confirm ARP behavior and that your routing design still allows the master to reach upstream networks. In mixed-vendor environments, VRRP often simplifies interoperability. VRRP vs HSRP — practical differences means vrrp is an open standard like hsrp in behavior but differs in virtual mac format and the master's ability to use its physical ip for local traffic.. In practical terms, open standard vrrp compared to cisco hsrp behavior and use cases. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: VRRP difference
keyIdea.text: VRRP is an open standard like HSRP in behavior but differs in virtual MAC format and the master's ability to use its physical IP for local traffic.

content.html:
Comparison

VRRP vs HSRP

VRRP is the open standard alternative to HSRP; choose it for multi‑vendor interoperability and slightly different operational semantics.

Master vs Active
VRRP master can retain use of its physical IP; HSRP active primarily forwards for virtual IP.
Virtual MAC format
VRRP uses 0000.5E00.01xx; HSRP uses 0000.0C07.ACxx where xx is group number.
Use case
Prefer VRRP when multiple vendors are present; prefer HSRP for Cisco‑only features and behaviors.
Practical checks
Priority and preempt: Configure to control master election and recovery.
Timers and hellos: Verify that hello intervals and hold times meet your availability requirements.
Interoperability: Test ARP behavior and ensure master reachability to upstream networks.
Takeaway

VRRP and HSRP deliver gateway redundancy; choose VRRP for open standards and HSRP when Cisco‑specific behavior is required.

screens.title: VRRP configuration example
screens.subtitle: Create a VRRP master/backup group with priority and preempt

narration.text: This configuration example shows VRRP commands on a client‑facing interface. You first set the interface IP, then create a vrrp group, assign the virtual IP, and set priority and preemption behavior. The vrrp command names the group and the virtual IP used by hosts as their default gateway. Priority controls master election; preemption lets a recovered higher priority router regain the master role. After configuration, use show vrrp brief to confirm group state, master identity, and virtual IP. An important verification detail is that VRRP uses a distinct virtual MAC and may have different default timers from HSRP, so if you are migrating or interoperating, verify that the behavior matches availability requirements. Also check that no ACLs block VRRP hellos and that authentication, if used, matches across routers. Testing failover by shutting an interface and observing master changes solidifies understanding; expect ARP behavior to update on clients as appropriate during transitions. VRRP configuration example means use vrrp commands to create a master for a virtual ip, set priority and preempt, and verify with show vrrp brief.. In practical terms, create a vrrp master/backup group with priority and preempt. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: VRRP config
keyIdea.text: Use vrrp commands to create a master for a virtual IP, set priority and preempt, and verify with show vrrp brief.

content.html:
Definition

VRRP configuration example

Example VRRP commands to create group 1 with a virtual IP and preemption enabled.

interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip address 192.168.1.10 255.255.255.0
 vrrp 1 ip 192.168.1.1
 vrrp 1 priority 120
 vrrp 1 preempt
Verify: show vrrp brief shows group, virtual IP, and master/backup roles.
Tip: When using VRRP in multi‑vendor environments, confirm hello intervals and timers match availability targets.
Notes
Authentication: If configured, ensure all VRRP routers share the same key to avoid group formation failures.
IP use: VRRP master may still use its physical IP for local traffic, which can simplify designs where the gateway should also be reachable by its own IP.
Key Takeaway

Use VRRP where open standard behavior and multi-vendor compatibility are required, and always verify timers and hello traffic.

screens.title: GLBP architecture and operation
screens.subtitle: Active Virtual Gateway, Active Virtual Forwarders, and multiple virtual MACs

narration.text: GLBP is a Cisco proprietary FHRP that provides both redundancy and active‑active load balancing for a single virtual IP. Instead of a single active router, GLBP elects an Active Virtual Gateway which answers ARP requests for the virtual IP. The AVG assigns different virtual MAC addresses to available routers called Active Virtual Forwarders. When a host ARPs for the gateway, the AVG responds with one of the virtual MACs in a round‑robin, weighted, or host‑dependent manner, distributing clients across AVFs. This design lets all routers forward traffic simultaneously, improving bandwidth utilization compared to active‑standby models. A critical point is that GLBP still uses a single virtual IP — clients simply learn different MACs for the same IP. When verifying GLBP, show glbp brief displays AVG/AVF roles and assigned virtual MACs. A common misconception is that GLBP requires different IPs per router; it does not. Instead, GLBP uses multiple virtual MACs for the same IP, enabling active‑active forwarding. Use GLBP where you need redundancy and to maximize gateway throughput across multiple routers. GLBP architecture and operation means glbp provides active‑active gateway load balancing by assigning multiple virtual macs for a single virtual ip via an avg and avfs.. In practical terms, active virtual gateway, active virtual forwarders, and multiple virtual macs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: GLBP core
keyIdea.text: GLBP provides active‑active gateway load balancing by assigning multiple virtual MACs for a single virtual IP via an AVG and AVFs.

content.html:
Architecture

GLBP architecture and operation

GLBP elects an AVG that assigns virtual MACs to AVFs so multiple routers forward for the same virtual IP.

AVG
Answers ARP for the virtual IP and assigns virtual MACs to AVFs.
AVF
Forwards traffic for its assigned virtual MAC; multiple AVFs can be active concurrently.
Load balancing
AVG can distribute MAC assignments round‑robin, weighted, or host‑dependent to balance client load.
Operational notes
Single virtual IP: Clients use the same gateway IP but learn different MACs, enabling active‑active forwarding.
Verification: show glbp brief and show glbp <group> detail show AVG, AVF and MAC assignments.
Use case: Ideal when you want to maximize gateway capacity and avoid idle standby routers.
Key Takeaway

GLBP allows multiple routers to actively forward for the same virtual IP by assigning distinct virtual MACs to clients.

screens.title: GLBP configuration example
screens.subtitle: Set the AVG, priorities, preempt and choose load‑balancing method

narration.text: Configuring GLBP follows a familiar pattern: assign the physical interface IP, declare the glbp group and virtual IP, then set priority and preempt. You also choose a load‑balancing method such as round‑robin. The AVG election uses priority, so set the preferred AVG with a higher priority and enable preempt if you want it to reclaim AVG duties after recovery. After configuration, use show glbp brief to see which router is AVG and which devices are AVFs along with their assigned virtual MACs. To validate load distribution, generate multiple client MACs or pings and observe that the AVG responds with different virtual MACs for the same virtual IP. A common configuration error is not matching load‑balancing mode across members, or leaving preempt off and expecting automatic return of leadership. Use the provided commands in the chapter example, and verify with show glbp <group> detail to inspect virtual MAC assignments and AVF forwarding status. This practical configuration makes GLBP effective for active‑active gateway designs. GLBP configuration example means configure glbp group with virtual ip, priority and preempt, and set load-balancing method to distribute clients across avfs.. In practical terms, set the avg, priorities, preempt and choose load‑balancing method. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: GLBP config
keyIdea.text: Configure glbp group with virtual IP, priority and preempt, and set load-balancing method to distribute clients across AVFs.

content.html:
Process Flow

GLBP configuration example

Configure the interface, add the glbp group and virtual IP, set priority and preempt, then select a load‑balancing mode.

interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip address 192.168.1.10 255.255.255.0
 glbp 1 ip 192.168.1.1
 glbp 1 priority 120
 glbp 1 preempt
 glbp 1 load-balancing round-robin
Verify: show glbp brief to see AVG/AVF roles and virtual MAC assignments.
Tip: To observe distribution, generate traffic from multiple client MAC addresses and inspect show glbp <group> detail.
Troubleshooting
Missing preempt: AVG roles may not return automatically if preempt is not configured.
Mode mismatch: Ensure load-balancing method is compatible across group members to avoid uneven client distribution.
ARP observation: Verify clients learn different virtual MACs for the same virtual IP during distribution tests.
Key Takeaway

GLBP lets you use all gateway routers actively; verify MAC distribution to confirm load balancing is working as expected.

screens.title: Troubleshooting FHRP failures
screens.subtitle: Checks, show commands, common misconfigurations and symptoms

narration.text: Troubleshooting FHRPs starts with simple checks and progresses to verifying control traffic. First, confirm interface IP configuration and matching group numbers across routers. Next, use the show commands described in the chapter: show standby brief for HSRP, show vrrp brief for VRRP, and show glbp brief for GLBP to verify roles and virtual IPs. Inspect detailed outputs to see virtual MACs, priorities, preemption state, and tracking status. Common root causes include blocked hello packets — ensure ACLs or firewalls are not filtering FHRP UDP hellos — and mismatched authentication strings which prevent routers from joining the same group. Another frequent issue is forgetting preempt, which means a recovered higher‑priority router will not retake the active role until manually forced. Interface tracking misconfiguration can also cause either unnecessary failovers or prevent failovers when needed. For GLBP, verify that the AVG responds to ARP and that AVFs are forwarding for their assigned virtual MACs; if clients see only one MAC, load balancing is not occurring. A stepwise approach—verify config, check hellos, inspect show outputs, simulate a failure—helps isolate the fault quickly and reliably.

keyIdea.title: Troubleshooting steps
keyIdea.text: Verify interfaces, group numbers, hellos, authentication, priorities, preemption, and tracking. Use the show brief commands to locate issues quickly.

content.html:
Process Flow

Troubleshooting FHRP failures

A structured checklist reduces mean time to repair for FHRP issues.

  1. Validate interface IPs and matching FHRP group numbers.
  2. Check show standby/vrrp/glbp brief for roles, virtual IP, and MACs.
  3. Confirm preempt and priority values are as intended.
  4. Ensure hellos are not blocked by ACLs or firewall rules.
  5. Verify authentication strings if used, and inspect tracking settings.
Quick commands
show standby brief
show vrrp brief
show glbp brief
show glbp 3 detail
Interpretation: Look for expected active/master/AVG roles, virtual MACs, and whether preemption or tracking has modified priorities.
Common mistake

Forgetting to enable preempt makes a recovered higher priority router remain standby until manual action.

narration.text: This hands‑on scenario sets two routers R1 and R2 to provide redundant and load‑balanced default gateway services for the 192.168.1.0/24 network. On R1 you will configure the physical IP 192.168.1.10, HSRP group 1 virtual IP 192.168.1.254 with priority 110 and preempt, VRRP group 2 virtual IP 192.168.1.253 with lower VRRP priority so R2 becomes master, and GLBP group 3 virtual IP 192.168.1.252 with priority 110 as AVG. On R2 you will configure its physical IP 192.168.1.20, lower HSRP priority so it is standby, higher VRRP priority so it becomes master, and GLBP with lower priority so R1 remains AVG. After configuration, verify roles using show standby brief, show vrrp brief and show glbp brief from each router. Then simulate failures by shutting the client interface on R1 and observe failover, and bring it back to see preemption behavior. For GLBP, generate multiple client ARP requests or pings and inspect show glbp 3 detail to see which AVF handles which virtual MAC. This stepwise lab reinforces configuration, verification, and troubleshooting workflows you will rely on in the field. Lab scenario: Configure R1 and R2

Starter configurations for R1 and R2 covering HSRP, VRRP and GLBP according to the lab instructions.

R1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.1.10 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# standby 1 ip 192.168.1.254
R1(config-if)# standby 1 priority 110
R1(config-if)# standby 1 preempt
R1(config-if)# vrrp 2 ip 192.168.1.253

R2(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/1

R2(config-if)# vrrp 2 preempt

R2(config-if)# glbp 3 load-balancing round-robin
Verification checklist
  • Run show standby brief on R1 and R2 to confirm HSRP group 1 active/standby and virtual IP 192.168.1.254.
  • Run show vrrp brief to confirm VRRP group 2 master/backup for virtual IP 192.168.1.253.
  • Run show glbp brief and show glbp 3 detail to observe AVG, AVFs and virtual MAC assignments for 192.168.1.252.
  • Simulate failures by shutting the client interface on R1 and observe failover and then recovery with preemption enabled.
Why this matters

Combining HSRP, VRRP, and GLBP knowledge prepares you to design resilient gateways and validate their operation via practical lab steps.

screens.title: Testing and observing failover behavior
screens.subtitle: Simulate failures, observe preemption and GLBP MAC distribution

narration.text: Validation is as important as configuration. After you configure HSRP, VRRP, and GLBP, perform controlled tests to confirm expected behavior. Start by using show standby brief, show vrrp brief and show glbp brief to capture baseline states: active/master/AVG and virtual IPs. To test failover, administratively shut the client-facing interface on the intended primary router or use interface shutdown; observe that the standby/master/AVF takes over and client connectivity continues. For HSRP and VRRP, verify role transitions and ensure preemption permissions let a recovered higher‑priority router retake the active role if needed. For GLBP, generate multiple client ARP requests or pings from different client MACs and inspect show glbp <group> detail — you should see virtual MAC assignments distributed among AVFs. Watch the switch MAC table to confirm the virtual MAC moves or multiple virtual MACs exist for the same IP. Common mistakes during tests include forgetting to re-enable preempt so leadership does not return and forgetting that ACLs may block FHRP hellos; always verify control traffic flow. Finish by bringing interfaces back up and confirming the network returns to the designed steady state.

keyIdea.text: Use controlled shutdowns and show commands to verify failover, preemption behavior, and GLBP virtual MAC distribution across AVFs.

content.html:
Verification

Testing and observing failover behavior

Run a sequence of checks and controlled failures to confirm your FHRP setup behaves as intended in real events.

Baseline: show standby brief, show vrrp brief, show glbp brief to capture current roles and virtual IPs.
Failover test: shut the client interface on the primary and observe role change and continued client connectivity.
GLBP distribution: generate traffic from multiple clients and run show glbp <group> detail to see AVF virtual MAC assignments.
Checks & Validation
Observe switch MAC table entries to see virtual MACs associated with the client VLAN after failover.
Confirm that preemption behavior returns leadership if desired, and that tracking produced expected priority changes.
If behavior differs, re-check group numbers, authentication, and that hellos are not blocked.
Final takeaway

Testing with simulated failures and checking show outputs is the only reliable way to confirm your FHRP configuration meets availability goals.

narration.text: These key concepts are the mental anchors you should carry forward. FHRP stands for First Hop Redundancy Protocol and is the category of protocols that provide default gateway redundancy so hosts keep connectivity even when a physical router fails. A Virtual IP Address is the logical gateway address configured on FHRP group members that hosts use as their default gateway. A Virtual MAC Address is the L2 identity used by FHRP so switches can forward traffic consistently during a router takeover. Keep these definitions in mind as you design, configure, and verify redundancy; they explain how hosts remain unaware of router transitions and why ARP and switch MAC tables are central to validation. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Key Concepts
FHRP
Protocols that provide default gateway redundancy to eliminate a single point of failure.
Virtual IP Address
A logical gateway IP shared by group members that hosts use as their default gateway.
Virtual MAC Address
A logical MAC used by the virtual router so switches forward traffic correctly during failover.
Summary

These three concepts form the L3 and L2 basis of FHRP behavior; validating both layers is required to confirm resilient gateway operation.

narration.text: Remember these practical protocol and operational points. HSRP is Cisco proprietary and uses an active/standby model with a virtual MAC format tied to the HSRP group. VRRP is an open standard similar to HSRP but with a different virtual MAC format and with the master allowed to use its physical IP for local traffic. GLBP provides active‑active gateway load balancing by assigning multiple virtual MACs to different routers; an AVG answers ARP and assigns AVFs. Also remember preemption allows a higher‑priority router to resume active duties after recovery, and interface tracking lets a router's priority be dynamically reduced when a monitored interface fails. Finally, verification commands—show standby brief, show vrrp brief, and show glbp brief—are your first line of evidence for correct behavior. Keep these reminders close when you design, configure, and troubleshoot gateway redundancy in enterprise networks.

keyIdea.title: Protocols & features
keyIdea.text: HSRP, VRRP and GLBP differ in vendor scope and forwarding models; use preempt and tracking wisely and verify with the show commands.

content.html:
HSRP
Cisco proprietary active/standby protocol with virtual MAC 0000.0C07.ACxx.
VRRP
Open standard master/backup protocol using 0000.5E00.01xx virtual MAC format; good for multi‑vendor networks.
GLBP
Cisco proprietary active‑active gateway load balancing using an AVG and multiple virtual MACs for a single IP.
Summary takeaway

Pick the protocol that fits vendor constraints and performance needs, enable preempt and tracking where appropriate, and always verify using the show commands after any change.
